st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: Billups directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that AI does not displace a signing attorney’s personal, nondelegable duty of reasonable inquiry. kp.k: Unverified AI produced fabricated and misrepresented legal authorities
kp.d: The court found four problematic citations in the June 12, 2025 opposition memorandum: one nonexistent case and three existing cases whose holdings were misrepresented. Jane Watson admitted using Grok for research and drafting without verifying its output. This is a finding about specific filed work, not a measured model error rate.
qs: In total, there were four problematic citations identified in the Response Memorandum [65]:
She admitted that she used “Grok”, an external AI tool, to assist in drafting and research without verifying the accuracy of the output.

kp.k: AI verification failures disrupted litigation and consumed judicial resources
kp.d: The court attributed extensive research, delayed resolution of summary judgment and cancellation of the October 20, 2025 jury trial to the defective memorandum. Quoting Ferris, it emphasized the asymmetry between rapid production of false legal material and the work required of courts and opposing parties to detect it. The order identifies client delay, rather than only institutional inconvenience, as a central harm.
qs: This Court has wasted significant time and efforts sorting through this Memorandum [65] which contains blatant misrepresentations.
The case is at a standstill because of the egregious conduct at issue.
At the end of the day, it is not the Court who is the victim but the people whose day in court is endlessly delayed.

kp.k: Existing Rule 11 duties govern AI-assisted filings
kp.d: The court relied on Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 to sanction the conduct, while stating that it also considered the conduct sanctionable under its inherent authority. It applied an objective reasonable-inquiry standard at the time of signing, under which subjective good faith does not immunize counsel. Jane Watson's admitted failure to verify AI-generated authorities warranted sanctions.
qs: Although the Court is of the opinion that the subject conduct is sanctionable under its inherent authority, the Court need only rely on Rule 11 to impose the necessary sanctions in this case.
The Court finds that, through Ms. Watson’s own admission, she failed to verify the legal authorities generated by AI prior to filing the Memorandum [65] at issue.
This warrants Rule 11 sanctions.

kp.k: Supervising signatories cannot simply trust an associate's citations
kp.d: Norris reviewed and revised the memorandum's arguments but admitted not checking its citations. The court rejected his assumption that citations supplied by another attorney were accurate and found a Rule 11 violation. It stressed that Norris already knew of Watson's earlier unverified AI use. A case cited eight times was actually an irrelevant excessive-force and failure-to-train case, which the court said even cursory investigation would have exposed.
qs: Norris is a signatory to the Memorandum [65] and admitted that he failed to check the citations.
The Court finds that Norris violated Rule 11.
Despite having notice and appreciating the gravity of the situation, Norris continued to assume the accuracy of Ms. Watson’s citations.
A seasoned attorney examining the brief should have read a case so heavily relied upon.

kp.k: AI policy and training failed to prevent repeated misconduct
kp.d: After an opposing lawyer identified an earlier incident in March 2025, the firm restricted Jane Watson to its internal Smokeball tool, Archie, prohibited external AI and encouraged traditional research. All three lawyers also attended AI ethics CLE that month. The court found that Watson nevertheless continued using unverified AI, including in the June filing, and treated the prior notice, training and policy violations as aggravating circumstances.
qs: The Firm’s newly adopted AI policy limited Ms. Watson’s AI usage to “Archie” and banned the use of any external AI tool.
Of note, also in March 2025, the Firm’s three attorneys attended a continuing legal education (“CLE”) course on ethics in utilizing AI.
Ms. Watson wholly integrated unverified AI usage into her practice of law in blatant disregard of the Firm’s policy and her ethical obligations as an officer of the Court.

kp.k: Junior drafting remained subject to professional verification obligations
kp.d: Watson became an associate after admission to the Mississippi Bar in 2024 and primarily wrote briefs under Norris's supervision. She explained that she used AI while learning practice and trying to save time, and admitted assuming its research was accurate. The court treated this explanation as insufficient, especially given prior warnings; the account documents one junior lawyer's practice rather than establishing a general effect on junior employment or training.
qs: Ms. Watson worked primarily as a brief writer under Norris’ supervision.
I was lazy. I did not check my work.

kp.k: Firm responsibility extended beyond the individual drafter
kp.d: The court held Watson & Norris, PLLC jointly responsible under Rule 11(c)(1), finding no exceptional circumstances justifying exemption. Louis Watson neither drafted, reviewed nor signed the memorandum and was not found individually to have violated Rule 11 as a signatory, but the court emphasized his supervisory role and involvement in the earlier response to AI misuse. The firm's November 30, 2025 dissolution did not negate Norris's violations.
qs: Mr. Watson did not draft, review, or sign the Memorandum [65] at issue.
The Court finds that Mr. Watson did not individually violate Rule 11 as a signatory.
The Court does not find any exceptional circumstances that warrant the Firm’s exemption from being held jointly responsible for the Rule 11 violations.

kp.k: Incomplete remediation aggravated the court's concerns
kp.d: The firm reported identifying ten cases with unverified or inaccurate citations and seeking corrections, notifying opposing counsel and informing Billups. The court found its accounting unreliable: counsel reported four Northern District cases, whereas the court identified six, and the lawyers disagreed about whether eight or nine corrective motions had been filed. Despite nearly six weeks to prepare for the hearing, the court found that the firm had not established the reach of the harm.
qs: In reality, the Court has identified six cases in the Northern District where the Firm has admitted that it submitted filings containing misrepresentations of law due to unverified AI usage.
The Court appreciates the acceptance of responsibility and corrective measures but finds these efforts inadequate.

kp.k: Sanctions prioritized disqualification and disclosure over fines
kp.d: The court considered monetary sanctions and further training inadequate in these circumstances. It disqualified all three lawyers and their respective firms from representing Billups, stayed the case for 60 days to permit new counsel, and required disclosure of the order to judges in every pending state or federal case in which the lawyers were counsel of record. Jane Watson was also required to seek withdrawal from cases assigned to Judge Aycock and barred from entering other appearances before that judge for two years. The clerk was directed to send the order to the Mississippi Bar.
qs: The Court also finds that a monetary fine would not have a meaningful deterrent effect.
She shall not enter an appearance in any other case assigned to the undersigned for a period of two (2) years from today’s date.
This case is hereby STAYED for a period of 60 days to provide Billups an opportunity to obtain new counsel.

kp.k: Court-ordered audits made verification a retrospective institutional obligation
kp.d: The order required an internal audit within 60 days of all substantive filings bearing Jane Watson's signature since she became an associate, identifying affected cases, fabricated citations, misrepresented holdings and corrective actions. All three lawyers had to certify their review under oath. Norris was directed to provide an affidavit confirming that he had not used AI to draft filed briefs; otherwise, the audit would extend to cases with his signature within the previous two years. An incomplete or improper audit could trigger further sanctions.
qs: All three attorneys shall certify under oath that they reviewed all filings and identified all fictitious case citations and/or misrepresentations to the best of their ability.
Should this audit not be completed and/or be completed improperly, the Court will consider the same to be further sanctionable conduct.
If the Court is incorrect in that assumption, the audit requirement is hereby extended to all cases in which Norris has been a signatory on any filing within the last two years.

kp.k: Opposing parties were urged to flag AI misuse
kp.d: The court observed that LMSD could have identified the fabricated citation and misrepresented holdings in a reply or supplemental filing. It announced an expectation that all parties help detect AI misuse to preserve judicial integrity, without finding a Rule 11 violation by LMSD or imposing sanctions on it.
qs: Going forward, the Court expects all parties to assist in maintaining the integrity of the judicial process and to be diligent in flagging AI misuse.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Aycock presents unverified AI-assisted legal drafting as a source of fabricated authorities, misrepresented law, additional judicial work, litigation delays, and professional sanctions.
pts.d: The order finds that Jane Watson used Grok for research and drafting without checking its output and that supervising signatory Nick Norris failed to check the citations. It treats verification as a nondelegable professional responsibility rather than a task displaced by AI. The court also finds that the firm's AI policy and prior training failed to prevent repeated misuse. It imposes disqualification, disclosure to judges, an internal audit, and a two-year restriction on Jane Watson entering appearances before the issuing judge. Its conclusion that a monetary fine would not meaningfully deter misconduct is a case-specific prospective judgment, not an experimentally established finding. The order acknowledges potential benefits from prudent AI use by expressly adopting language from Ferris, but does not independently quantify those benefits.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on the court's examination of filings, counsel's hearing admissions, the firm's account of repeated incidents, and cited sanctions precedents—not model benchmarks or measured hallucination rates.
pts.d: In the memorandum at issue, the court identified one nonexistent case and three existing cases whose holdings were misrepresented. Jane Watson accepted the court's findings and admitted using unverified AI output. Norris admitted reviewing arguments without checking citations. The firm reported ten affected cases across two Mississippi federal districts, but the court challenged its geographic accounting: it identified six Northern District cases rather than the four reported by the firm. The order documents an inability to resolve summary judgment and cancellation of the scheduled trial. Rule 11 and earlier sanctions decisions supply the legal basis for responsibility and remedies. The order's broader claims about pressure on courts draw on judicial experience and cited incidents; it offers no systematic measure of nationwide prevalence or net productivity.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The order addresses misconduct during 2025 and conditions its principal warnings on reliance on AI output without verification, especially after prior notice.
pts.d: An opposing attorney alerted the firm to unverified AI use in March 2025, when all three attorneys also attended AI ethics training. The firm then restricted Jane Watson to its internal Archie tool and prohibited external AI tools. The challenged memorandum was filed on June 12, approximately three months after that warning. Show-cause proceedings followed in September and October, and sanctions were issued December 19, 2025. Repetition despite notice and ineffective corrective measures explain the severity of the sanctions. The order requires disclosure within 30 days and an audit within 60 days, stays the case for 60 days so Billups can obtain new counsel, and restricts Jane Watson's appearances before Judge Aycock for two years. These are immediate findings and forward-looking deterrence measures, not a forecast of AI adoption or market displacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The order identifies consequences for drafting associates, supervising lawyers, firms, opposing parties, courts, clients, and other people awaiting adjudication.
pts.d: The immediate provider is a three-lawyer plaintiff-side employment firm. Jane Watson faces sanctions for drafting and filing unverified material; Norris faces sanctions as a supervising signatory; Louis Watson is not found individually to have violated Rule 11 as a signatory to this memorandum, but is not absolved of responsibility, and the firm is held jointly responsible. All three attorneys are disqualified from this case. The audit and disclosure requirements impose additional review and compliance work. Opposing parties are expected to flag AI misuse, while the court describes its own substantial investigative burden. Billups experiences delay and must obtain replacement counsel or proceed without counsel. The court extends its concern to the public whose cases compete for limited judicial resources; this is a claim about delay and judicial capacity, not a quantified access-to-justice or legal-market finding.
